tagline: Across Kentucky’s hills, a highway links Shaker buildings and Ohio River towns
intro: US 68 winds through forested hills across much of its Kentucky course, becoming Harrodsburg Road and then Broadway in Lexington. The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet lists three scenic sections between Lebanon and Maysville totaling 103.809 miles, plus a separate Lebanon-to-Paducah designation. Shakertown Road at Pleasant Hill has its own 2.4-mile designation. The state’s inventory dates the western Lebanon–Paducah designation to December 15, 2008.

In 1830, President Andrew Jackson vetoed a bill allowing federal purchase of stock in the Maysville-Washington-Lexington Turnpike Road Company. The proposed road would have linked Lexington with Washington and the Ohio River at Maysville. The numbered highway has changed course: from 1926 into the late 1940s, US 68 traveled between Bowling Green and Perryville by way of Horse Cave and Bardstown. It shifted to its present routing around 1948–49, apart from the later Glasgow bypass. In the 1990s, widening between Cadiz and Bowling Green added bypasses at Hopkinsville and Russellville.

Travel east from Reidland through Cadiz and Bowling Green, then continue by Glasgow and Campbellsville toward Lebanon and Harrodsburg. Pleasant Hill lies southwest of Lexington. Beyond Lexington, the designated sections run through Paris and resume at the Licking River, continuing through Washington to Maysville and the Ohio state line.

moments.title: Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill
moments.text: At Pleasant Hill, the Shakers used horses to pump water into a tower in the early 1830s, then piped it to kitchens, cellars and wash houses. Their wash houses also had horse-powered washing machines. The community dissolved in 1910, though elderly members remained until Mary Settles died in 1923. A restoration effort led by Joseph Graves and Earl D. Wallace began in 1961. The village now has 34 original nineteenth-century buildings on 2,800 acres of farmland. By 1964, the Friends of Pleasant Hill had secured a $2 million federal loan to buy and restore the property.

moments.title: Blue Licks Battlefield
moments.text: A monument at Blue Licks commemorates the battle fought here on August 19, 1782. Major Hugh McGary led an immediate pursuit of British Captain William Caldwell’s retreating force, rather than waiting for reinforcements. Sixty of the 176 men who followed McGary died, including Daniel Boone’s son Israel; seven more were captured. The saltwater springs later supported a nineteenth-century health resort, but the last spring had dried up by 1896. The park lies along the Licking River, where a one-mile trail follows the riverbank. Salt making at the springs had begun in the 1770s, before the resort developed.
moments.notice: The park’s monument commemorates the August 19, 1782 battle.

moments.title: Washington
moments.text: In 1833, Harriet Beecher came to Washington to visit her student Elizabeth Key. Then a teacher at the Western Female Institute in Cincinnati, she witnessed a slave auction in front of the old courthouse. That experience, together with her other encounters with slavery, led her to write Uncle Tom’s Cabin after she became Harriet Beecher Stowe. The Key House on Main Street, where she stayed, now contains the Harriet Beecher Stowe Slavery to Freedom Museum. Washington became part of Maysville in 1990. Maysville had already replaced Washington as the Mason County seat in 1848, shifting county government to the Ohio River town.
